claim: The store-operated calcium channel Orai governs Ca2+ influx through the plasma membrane of many non-excitable cells in metazoans.
source: The store-operated calcium (Ca2+) channel Orai governs Ca2+ influx through the plasma membrane of many non-excitable cells in metazoans.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that represents established knowledge about Orai function.

claim: The Orai channel opens in response to the depletion of Ca2+ stored in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: The channel opens in response to the depletion of Ca2+ stored in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract describing the activation mechanism of Orai, which is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Loss- and gain-of-function mutants of Orai cause disease.
source: Loss- and gain-of-function mutants of Orai cause disease.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge and citations provided later in the manuscript.

claim: Previous work revealed the structure of Orai with a closed pore.
source: Our previous work revealed the structure of Orai with a closed pore.
evidence: This refers to prior published work by the authors, as evidenced by citations to Hou et al., 2012 throughout the manuscript.

claim: A gain-of-function mutation constitutively activates the Orai channel.
source: Here, using a gain-of-function mutation that constitutively activates the channel, we present an X-ray structure of Drosophila melanogaster Orai in an open conformation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing H206A activity.

claim: The X-ray structure of Drosophila melanogaster Orai in an open conformation has been determined.
source: Here, using a gain-of-function mutation that constitutively activates the channel, we present an X-ray structure of Drosophila melanogaster Orai in an open conformation.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the manuscript, supported by crystallographic data.

claim: The pore is dramatically dilated on its cytosolic side in the open conformation compared to the closed pore.
source: Well-defined electron density maps reveal that the pore is dramatically dilated on its cytosolic side in comparison to the slender closed pore.
evidence: This is supported by structural data from electron density maps and comparison with the closed structure.

claim: Cations and anions bind in different regions of the open pore.
source: Cations and anions bind in different regions of the open pore, informing mechanisms for ion permeation and Ca2+ selectivity.
evidence: This is supported by anomalous difference electron density data showing ion binding sites.

claim: Opening of the pore requires the release of cytosolic latches.
source: Opening of the pore requires the release of cytosolic latches.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparisons between different conformations and inference from the structural data.

claim: An unlatched-but-closed conformation of Orai exists.
source: Together with additional X-ray structures of an unlatched-but-closed conformation, we propose a sequence for store-operated activation.
evidence: This is supported by X-ray structures of WT and K163W Oraicryst presented in the manuscript.

claim: Transient increases in cytosolic calcium concentration relay internal messages and enable cells to respond to external stimuli.
source: The dearth of calcium (Ca2+) ions in the cytosol of non-excitable metazoan cells under 'resting' conditions allows transient increases in the cytosolic calcium concentration to relay internal messages and enables cells to respond to external stimuli.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell biology, supported by the citation to Clapham, 2007.

claim: Cytosolic calcium signals regulate gene transcription, cell motility, exocytosis, and cell metabolism.
source: These cytosolic calcium signals regulate a plethora of processes including gene transcription, cell motility, exocytosis, and cell metabolism (Clapham, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Short-lived increases in cytosolic [Ca2+] can be generated by the release of Ca2+ from the endoplasmic reticulum through IP3R channels.
source: Short-lived increases in cytosolic [Ca2+] can be generated by the release of Ca2+ into the cytosol from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) through ion channels such as the IP3R channel (Clapham, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A more long-lasting elevation in cytosolic calcium occurs by the opening of Orai channels in the plasma membrane.
source: A second, more long-lasting elevation in cytosolic calcium occurs by the opening of Orai channels in the plasma membrane that allow Ca2+ ions to flow into the cell (Hogan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The driving force for Ca2+ entry through Orai is substantial due to negative voltage inside the cell and the chemical gradient.
source: The driving force for Ca2+ entry is substantial: the negative voltage inside the cell is an attractive force and in the same direction as the chemical gradient for Ca2+ – approximately 2 mM [Ca2+] outside the cell and 20,000–fold lower inside the cell (~100 nM).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cellular Ca2+ gradients and electrochemical driving forces.

claim: Orai conducts ions approximately 100-times slower than most Ca2+ channels.
source: Despite these driving forces, Orai conducts ions approximately 100-times slower than most Ca2+ channels (Orai has a single channel conductance of only ~20 fS [Prakriya and Lewis, 2006])
evidence: This is supported by citation to published electrophysiological measurements.

claim: Orai has a single channel conductance of only ~20 fS.
source: Orai has a single channel conductance of only ~20 fS [Prakriya and Lewis, 2006]
evidence: This is a specific measurement from cited literature.

claim: The slow conductance of Orai prevents overwhelming the cell with Ca2+ when the channel opens.
source: this probably serves important physiological roles: it would prevent overwhelming the cell with Ca2+ when the channel opens and would restrict the Ca2+ elevation to a small region around the channel.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the physiological significance of Orai's low conductance.

claim: Orai is one of the most Ca2+-selective channels known.
source: Orai is one of the most Ca2+-selective channels known and the structure of an opened pore could also provide insight into how the channel achieves such exquisite selectivity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Orai's selectivity properties.

claim: Calcium influx through Orai is necessary for activation of immune response genes in T cells.
source: Calcium influx through Orai is necessary for activation of immune response genes in T cells and a range of other physiological processes (Feske et al., 2005; Lacruz and Feske, 2015; Prakriya and Lewis, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in Orai cause immune system dysfunction, including severe combined immunodeficiency-like disorders.
source: Generally, loss-of-function mutations cause immune system dysfunction, including severe combined immunodeficiency-like disorders (Feske et al., 2006; Lacruz and Feske, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Gain-of-function mutations of Orai result in constitutive activation of the channel and have been associated with tubular aggregate myopathy and Stormorken syndromes.
source: Gain-of-function mutations of Orai have also been identified. These result in constitutive activation of the channel and have been associated with tubular aggregate myopathy and Stormorken syndromes (Lacruz and Feske, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: There are three Orai proteins in humans (Orai1-3).
source: There are three Orai proteins in humans (Orai1-3).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Orai protein family.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster contains one Orai ortholog that shares 73% sequence identity to human Orai1 in the transmembrane region.
source: Drosophila melanogaster contains one ortholog (Orai), which shares 73% sequence identity to human Orai1 in the transmembrane region, and is the most studied non-human Orai channel.
evidence: This is a factual statement about sequence identity that can be verified by sequence alignment.

claim: Orai channels have broad tissue distribution and are tightly regulated.
source: The channels have broad tissue distribution and are tightly regulated (Hogan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In the quiescent state before activation, the ion pore of Orai is closed to prevent aberrant Ca2+ flux through the plasma membrane.
source: In the quiescent state before activation, the ion pore of Orai is closed to prevent aberrant Ca2+ flux through the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Orai regulation.

claim: The channel is activated by the depletion of Ca2+ from the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: The channel is activated by the depletion of Ca2+ from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), and as such it was characterized as the calcium release-activated calcium (CRAC) channel responsible for store-operated calcium entry (SOCE) before the molecular components were known (Hoth and Penner, 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Orai was identified as the protein that forms the CRAC channel's pore.
source: Orai was identified as the protein that forms the channel's pore and STIM was identified as its regulator (Feske et al., 2006; Liou et al., 2005; Prakriya et al., 2006; Roos et al., 2005; Vig et al., 2006a; Yeromin et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: STIM was identified as the regulator of Orai.
source: Orai was identified as the protein that forms the channel's pore and STIM was identified as its regulator (Feske et al., 2006; Liou et al., 2005; Prakriya et al., 2006; Roos et al., 2005; Vig et al., 2006a; Yeromin et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: As a result of depletion of Ca2+ within the ER, STIM localizes to regions where the ER and plasma membranes are separated by only 10–20 nM.
source: As a result of depletion of Ca2+ within the ER, STIM, which is a single-pass membrane protein resident to the ER, localizes to regions where the ER and plasma membranes are separated by only 10–20 nM.
evidence: This is established knowledge about STIM localization upon ER Ca2+ depletion.

claim: STIM physically interacts with cytosolic regions of Orai to open its pore.
source: Here, STIM physically interacts with cytosolic regions of Orai to open its pore.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of Orai activation.

claim: The X-ray structure of Drosophila melanogaster Orai in a 'quiescent' conformation with a closed ion pore was previously determined.
source: We previously determined the X-ray structure of Drosophila melanogaster Orai in a 'quiescent' conformation with a closed ion pore (Hou et al., 2012).
evidence: This refers to prior published work by the authors.

claim: The channel is formed from an assembly of six Orai subunits that surround a single ion pore.
source: The channel is formed from an assembly of six Orai subunits that surround a single ion pore, which is perpendicular to the plasma membrane in a cellular setting (Figure 1A) (Hou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by structural data from the previous structure and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The functional state of human Orai1 is as a hexamer of subunits.
source: Although the oligomeric state revealed by the X-ray structure was a surprise, further studies have shown that the functional state of human Orai1 is also as a hexamer of subunits (Cai et al., 2016; Yen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to other studies.

claim: Each Orai subunit contains four transmembrane helices (M1-M4) and a cytosolic M4-ext helix.
source: Each Orai subunit contains four transmembrane helices (M1-M4) and a cytosolic M4-ext helix (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Amino acid side chains on the M1 helices from the six subunits form the walls of the pore.
source: Amino acid side chains on the M1 helices from the six subunits form the walls of the pore (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Amino acid side chains establish the dimensions and chemical environment along the entirety of the pore.
source: In contrast to many ion channels, amino acid side chains establish the dimensions and chemical environment along the entirety of the pore.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural data showing that M1 helices line the pore.

claim: The M2 and M3 helices form a shell surrounding the M1 helices and shield them from the membrane.
source: The M2 and M3 helices form a shell surrounding the M1 helices and shield them from the membrane.
evidence: This is supported by structural data from the quiescent conformation.

claim: The M4 helices are located at the periphery and contain two segments, M4a and M4b, delineated by a bend at a conserved proline residue (Pro288).
source: The M4 helices are located at the periphery and contain two segments, M4a and M4b, delineated by a bend at a conserved proline residue (Pro288).
evidence: This is supported by structural data from the quiescent conformation.

claim: The M4-ext helices from neighboring subunits interact with one another through pairwise helical coiled-coil packing.
source: Following M4b, the M4-ext helices extend into cytosol. The M4-ext helices from neighboring subunits interact with one another through pairwise helical coiled-coil packing, which creates a belt-like arrangement surrounding the channel on its intracellular side (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Mutation of the hydrophobic residues that mediate the coiled-coils prevents channel activation by STIM.
source: Mutation of the hydrophobic residues that mediate the coiled-coils has been shown to prevent channel activation by STIM, possibly by reducing the affinity for STIM (Muik et al., 2008; Navarro-Borelly et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: The cytosolic domain of STIM contains coiled-coil regions.
source: Because the cytosolic domain of STIM also contains coiled-coil regions (Fahrner et al., 2014; Stathopulos et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2012), it has been proposed that STIM interacts with the M4-ext helices through a coiled-coil interaction
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: STIM interacts with the M4-ext helices through a coiled-coil interaction.
source: it has been proposed that STIM interacts with the M4-ext helices through a coiled-coil interaction and that the structure represents a quiescent conformation prior to the binding of STIM (Hou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural features and cited literature.

claim: The closed pore is approximately 55 Å long, narrow, and impermeant to ions.
source: The X-ray structure of the quiescent conformation of Orai revealed that the closed pore is approximately 55 Å long, narrow, and impermeant to ions (Figure 1B) (Hou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by structural data from the quiescent conformation.

claim: The closed pore contains four sections: a glutamate ring on the extracellular side that forms the selectivity filter, a ~15 Å-long hydrophobic section, a ~15 Å-long basic section, and a cytosolic section.
source: It contains four sections: a glutamate ring on the extracellular side that forms the selectivity filter (comprising Glu178 residues from the six subunits), a ~15 Å-long hydrophobic section, a ~15 Å-long basic section, and a cytosolic section (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mutation of Glu106 in human Orai1 (corresponding to Glu178 in Drosophila Orai) to aspartate disrupts Ca2+-selectivity.
source: Mutation of the residue corresponding to Glu178 in human Orai1 (Glu106) to aspartate disrupts Ca2+-selectivity (Prakriya et al., 2006; Vig et al., 2006b; Yeromin et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: The walls of the basic section are formed by three amino acids from each of the six M1 helices that are conserved as lysine or arginine in Orai channels.
source: The walls of the basic section are formed by three amino acids from each of the six M1 helices that are conserved as lysine or arginine in Orai channels (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by structural data and sequence conservation analysis.

claim: The R91W mutation in human Orai1 (corresponding to K163W in Drosophila Orai) causes a severe combined immune deficiency-like disorder by preventing channel activation.
source: Mutation of the top basic residue in human Orai1 (R91W, corresponding to K163W in Drosophila Orai) causes a severe combined immune deficiency-like disorder by preventing channel activation (Derler et al., 2009; Feske et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical and functional studies.

claim: The presence of 18 basic residues within the pore of a cation channel is highly unusual.
source: The presence of 18 basic residues (three from each of the six subunits) within the pore of a cation channel is highly unusual and would presumably establish an electrostatic barrier that opposes Ca2+ permeation in the closed state.
evidence: This is an inference based on electrostatic principles and the structural observation.

claim: The closed conformation of the basic region serves as a binding site for anions that stabilize the arginine/lysine residues in close proximity.
source: We found that the closed conformation of the basic region serves as a binding site for anion(s) that stabilize the arginine/lysine residues in close proximity (Hou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by structural data from the previous study.

claim: An iron complex co-purifies with the channel and binds at the center of the basic residues in the closed pore.
source: In the structure, an iron complex that co-purifies with the channel, which may be (FeCl6)3-, binds at the center of the basic residues like a plug.
evidence: This is supported by anomalous difference electron density data from the previous structure.

claim: Certain mutations of M1 residues that line the pore create constitutively active channels but these channels have reduced selectivity for Ca2+ compared to STIM-activated Orai.
source: Certain mutations of M1 residues that line the pore create constitutively active channels but these channels have reduced selectivity for Ca2+ in comparison to STIM-activated Orai, which suggests that their pores have non-native conformations (McNally et al., 2012; Yamashita et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: The high selectivity and normal inwardly rectifying current-voltage relationship of the H134A mutant suggest that this mutation induces a conformation of the pore that is highly similar to the conformation of the pore when Orai is activated by STIM.
source: The high selectivity and the normal inwardly rectifying current-voltage relationship of the H134A mutant suggest that this mutation induces a conformation of the pore that is highly similar to the conformation of the pore when Orai is activated by STIM (Frischauf et al., 2017; Yeung et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on functional properties and supported by citations.

claim: The H206A mutation in Drosophila Orai (corresponding to H134A in human Orai1) generates a constitutively active channel.
source: In this study, we introduced the corresponding amino acid substitution into Drosophila Orai (H206A), confirmed that it generates a constitutively active channel, and determined its X-ray structure.
evidence: This is supported by functional data presented in the manuscript (Figure 3).

claim: Oraicryst-RR and Oraicryst with a wild-type M3-M4 loop operate as CRAC channels that can be activated by STIM.
source: We find that both the previously crystallized construct and one with a wild-type M3-M4 loop operate as CRAC channels that can be activated by STIM (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by functional data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The constructs used for crystallization possess the fundamental properties of previously studied Orai channels.
source: Thus, the constructs used for crystallization possess the fundamental properties of previously studied Orai channels.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the functional data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Robust K+ flux through H206A Oraicryst was observed under divalent-free conditions.
source: Using divalent-free conditions, under which ionic currents through CRAC channels are more easily observed due to greater conductance of monovalent cations (e.g. Na+ or K+) than Ca2+ (Lepple-Wienhues and Cahalan, 1996; Prakriya and Lewis, 2006), we observed robust K+ flux through the channel.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Ion flux was not observed for empty vesicles or through WT Oraicryst without STIM activation.
source: Ion flux was not observed for empty vesicles or through a channel without the H206A mutation (WT Oraicryst), as is expected without activation by STIM (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: K+ flux through H206A Oraicryst was blocked by the addition of Gd3+.
source: Similar to wild-type CRAC channels, K+ flux was blocked by the addition of Gd3+ (Figure 3C) (Yeromin et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: K+ flux through H206A Oraicryst was inhibited by the addition of Mg2+ or Ca2+.
source: K+ flux through H206A Oraicryst was also inhibited by the addition of Mg2+ or Ca2+ (Figure 3C), which is in accord with the properties exhibited by STIM-activated channels and indicative of the channel's selectivity for Ca2+ (Lepple-Wienhues and Cahalan, 1996; Prakriya and Lewis, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: H206A Oraicryst forms an open channel that recapitulates properties of STIM-activated Orai.
source: Thus, as has been shown for the corresponding H134A mutation of human Orai1 (Frischauf et al., 2017; Yeung et al., 2018), H206A Oraicryst forms an open channel that recapitulates properties of STIM-activated Orai.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the functional data and comparison with cited literature.

claim: Crystals of H206A Oraicryst were improved from an initial diffraction limit of 20 Å resolution to 6.7 Å resolution through extensive optimization.
source: Extensive optimization of crystallization conditions improved the quality of H206A Oraicryst crystals from an initial diffraction limit of 20 Å resolution to 6.7 Å resolution.
evidence: This describes the experimental process of crystal optimization.

claim: The asymmetric unit of H206A Oraicryst crystals contains 24 Orai subunits arranged as four complete channels.
source: In this case, the asymmetric unit contains 24 Orai subunits, which are arranged as four complete channels.
evidence: This is a crystallographic observation from the diffraction data.

claim: 24-fold non-crystallographic symmetry allowed accurate determination of crystallographic phases and obtaining electron density maps of excellent quality.
source: The 24-fold non-crystallographic symmetry allowed us to accurately determine the crystallographic phases and obtain electron density maps of excellent quality, which delineate all α-helices of the channel and resemble maps calculated using considerably higher resolution diffraction data (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—video 1, Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the crystallographic method and is supported by the electron density maps shown in Figure 4.

claim: All four channels in the asymmetric unit adopt the same conformation.
source: All four channels in the asymmetric unit adopt the same conformation.
evidence: This is an observation from the structural data.

claim: Anomalous-difference electron-density peaks corresponding to methionine and cysteine residues indicate the validity of the atomic model and the accuracy of the crystallographic phases.
source: Anomalous-difference electron-density peaks corresponding to these amino acids indicate both the validity of the atomic model and the accuracy of the crystallographic phases that were used to generate the electron density maps of the channel (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by anomalous difference electron density data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The X-ray structure of H206A Oraicryst reveals a new conformation of the channel with a dilated pore that presumably represents an open conformation.
source: The X-ray structure of H206A Oraicryst reveals a new conformation of the channel with a dilated pore that presumably represents an open conformation (Figure 4).
evidence: This is the main structural finding, supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The open channel is composed of a hexameric assembly of Orai subunits surrounding a single ion pore.
source: The open channel is composed of a hexameric assembly of Orai subunits surrounding a single ion pore (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The overall architecture of the open channel is similar to the quiescent conformation.
source: The overall architecture of the channel is similar to the quiescent conformation, with each Orai subunit containing four transmembrane helices (M1-M4).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the two structures.

claim: The six M1 helices form the walls of the open pore.
source: The six M1 helices, one contributed by each subunit of the channel, form the walls of the open pore.
evidence: This is supported by structural data.

claim: The pore is dramatically dilated on its cytosolic end in the open conformation, expanding by ~10 Å at Lys159 compared to the closed pore.
source: In comparison to the closed pore (Hou et al., 2012), the pore is dramatically dilated on its cytosolic end, expanding by ~10 Å at Lys159 (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 5.

claim: The differences between the closed and open pores taper off toward the extracellular side.
source: The differences between the closed and open pores taper off toward the extracellular side such that, while subtle changes may occur when the pore opens, the location of the M1 helix at Glu178 is indistinguishable from the closed conformation at this resolution.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison between the open and closed conformations.

claim: The principal conformational change in the pore results from an outward rigid body rotation of the M1-M4a portion of each subunit away from the central axis and a slight additional outward bend of M1 on its intracellular half.
source: The electron density indicates that the principal conformational change in the pore results from an outward rigid body rotation of the M1-M4a portion of each subunit away from the central axis and a slight additional outward bend of M1 on its intracellular half (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The packing of M1-M4a within an individual subunit is nearly indistinguishable from the packing in the closed conformation.
source: The packing of M1-M4a within an individual subunit is nearly indistinguishable from the packing in the closed conformation (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The rigid body motion suggests that the amino acids on M1 that form the walls of the pore in the closed conformation also do so in the open conformation.
source: The rigid body motion suggests that the amino acids on M1 that form the walls of the pore in the closed conformation also do so in the open conformation Figure 4B and Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation of rigid body motion.

claim: The exposure of M1 residues to the ion pore in its open conformation is consistent with accessibility experiments of cysteine residues introduced into the M1 helix by mutagenesis.
source: The exposure of these residues to the ion pore in its open conformation is consistent with accessibility experiments of cysteine residues introduced into the M1 helix by mutagenesis (McNally et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by comparison with cited functional studies.

claim: Residue 206 is located on the M2 helix and does not line the pore.
source: Residue 206 is located on the M2 helix and does not line the pore (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In the quiescent conformation, His206 forms a hydrogen bond with the side chain of Ser165.
source: In the quiescent conformation, the wild-type histidine at this position forms a hydrogen bond with the side chain of Ser165, which is located on the side of M1 facing away from the pore (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) (Hou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by structural data from the quiescent conformation shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A histidine could be accommodated in the open conformation without steric interference.
source: On the basis of the current structure, a histidine could be accommodated in the open conformation without steric interference, suggesting that the conformation of the pore observed for H206A Oraicryst could be adopted by wild-type Orai (e.g. when activated by STIM, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural modeling shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Interactions between non-pore-lining regions of the channel influence pore opening.
source: In accord with previous studies (Frischauf et al., 2017; Yeung et al., 2018), we surmise that interactions between non-pore-lining regions of the channel (e.g. M2-M1 interactions) influence pore opening.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation and cited literature.

claim: Anomalous-difference electron density maps contained strong density for Gd3+ and Ba2+ in the selectivity filter of the open pore.
source: Anomalous-difference electron density maps, which pinpoint the location of these ions, contained strong density for Gd3+ and for Ba2+ in the selectivity filter (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by anomalous difference electron density data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: The electron densities for Ba2+/Gd3+ could represent one or two ions that directly coordinate the side chains of the glutamate ring.
source: Due to the limited resolution of the diffraction data, the electron densities could represent one or two Ba2+/Gd3+ ions that directly coordinate the side chains of the glutamate ring (Glu178 residues from the six subunits).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the electron density data considering the resolution limits.

claim: The presence of Ba2+ and Gd3+ in the selectivity filter provides evidence that the Glu178 side chains are oriented toward the pore when it is open.
source: The presence of Ba2+ and Gd3+ at this location provide evidence that the Glu178 side chains are oriented toward the pore when it is open.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ion binding data.

claim: Ca2+-binding in the selectivity filter region likely underlies Orai's high selectivity for Ca2+.
source: Ca2+-binding in this region likely underlies Orai's high selectivity for Ca2+.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural observation of ion binding.

claim: Block of the open pore by Gd3+ appears to occur by competitive binding within the selectivity filter.
source: Block of the open pore by Gd3+ appears to occur by competitive binding within the selectivity filter.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Gd3+ binding data.

claim: Gd3+, Ba2+ and Ca2+ bind near the glutamate ring when the pore is closed.
source: We showed previously that Gd3+, Ba2+ and Ca2+ bind near the glutamate ring when the pore is closed (Hou et al., 2012).
evidence: This refers to findings from the previous structure.

claim: The positioning of Gd3+ is very similar between the open and closed pores.
source: While the positioning of Gd3+ is very similar between the open and closed pores, the positioning of Ba2+/Ca2+ is noticeably different (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of anomalous difference electron density maps shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the closed pore, Ba2+/Ca2+ binds on the extracellular side of the selectivity filter, approximately 4 Å above the ring of glutamates.
source: In the closed pore, the Ba2+/Ca2+ ion binds on the extracellular side of the selectivity filter, approximately 4 Å above the ring of glutamates, whereas in the open pore, the electron density is located within the glutamate ring rather than above it (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of ion binding positions shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The apparent repositioning of Ba2+ indicates that subtle changes within the selectivity filter occur when the pore opens.
source: The limits of the diffraction data prevent us from discerning differences in the conformations of the glutamate side chains between the open and closed pores but the apparent repositioning of Ba2+ is an indication that subtle changes within the selectivity filter occur when the pore opens.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences in Ba2+ positioning.

claim: Subtle changes at the extracellular side of the pore have been suggested by spectroscopic and electrophysiological studies when Orai is activated by STIM.
source: Subtle changes at the extracellular side of the pore have also been suggested by spectroscopic and electrophysiological studies when Orai is activated by STIM (Gudlur et al., 2014; McNally et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to other studies.

claim: The transition between non-conductive and conductive conformations involves conformational changes along the length of the pore that introduce functionally important free-energy differences affecting Ca2+ selectivity and ion flow.
source: We conclude that the transition in the pore between non-conductive and conductive conformations involves conformational changes along the length of the pore that introduce functionally important free-energy differences that affect Ca2+ selectivity and ion flow.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural observations and ion binding data.

claim: These conformational changes are most structurally pronounced at the cytoplasmic side but extend energetically to the selectivity filter on the extracellular side.
source: These changes are most structurally pronounced at the cytoplasmic side but they extend energetically to the selectivity filter on the extracellular side.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural observations.

claim: Anomalous difference electron density for iron is not observed in the structure of H206A Oraicryst.
source: Anomalous difference electron density for iron is not observed in the structure of H206A Oraicryst, indicating that the iron complex is not present in the open pore, which is in accord with the dramatic widening of the basic region.
evidence: This is an observation from the anomalous difference electron density data.

claim: Robust anomalous difference electron density for I- was observed centrally located within the basic region of the open pore.
source: We observed robust anomalous difference electron density for I- that is centrally located within the basic region of the open pore (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by anomalous difference electron density data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The presence of I- in the basic region provides evidence that the basic amino acids are exposed to the pore and that anions can bind in the basic region when it is open.
source: The presence of I- there provides evidence that the basic amino acids are exposed to the pore and that anion(s) can bind in the basic region when it is open.
evidence: This is an inference based on the I- binding data.

claim: In the open conformation, the basic region is large enough to accommodate a centrally located Ca2+ ion surrounded by anions and/or water molecules.
source: In the open conformation, the basic region is large enough to accommodate a centrally located Ca2+ ion that is surrounded by anions and/or water molecules. (The Cα positions of Lys159 residues on opposite sides of the pore are ~24 Å apart).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural dimensions of the open pore.

claim: Cellular anions may shield the positive charge of the basic residues during the permeation of Ca2+ through the open pore.
source: We hypothesize that cellular anions may shield the positive charge of the basic residues during the permeation of Ca2+ through the open pore.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural observations and anion binding data.

claim: SSS Oraicryst (with R155S, K159S, K163S mutations) does not show ion flux in proteoliposome assays.
source: However, we did not detect ion flux through SSS Oraicryst, suggesting that is not constitutively open (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: SSS Oraicryst exhibits a monodisperse size-exclusion chromatography profile analogous to protein used for X-ray structures.
source: This does not appear to be due to gross misfolding of the channel because protein solubilized by detergent from the proteoliposomes exhibits a monodisperse size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) profile that is analogous to the profile of protein that was used to determine the X-ray structures (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Orai channels with the R155S/K159S/K163S (SSS) mutations do not form functional CRAC channels when co-expressed with STIM in HEK293 cells.
source: Furthermore, we find that Orai channels with the R155S/K159S/K163S (SSS) mutations do not form functional CRAC channels when co-expressed with STIM in HEK293 cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by functional data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: SSS Orai is expressed in the plasma membrane of cells at a similar level to wild type Orai.
source: Flow cytometry using an antibody that binds to the extracellular side of Orai demonstrates that SSS Orai is expressed in the plasma membrane of the cells at a similar level to wild type Orai and SEC suggests that SSS Orai is properly folded in the cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,C,D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry and SEC data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The inability of SSS Orai to be activated by STIM could be due to constitutive closure of the pore and/or disruption of the interaction with STIM.
source: The inability of SSS Orai to be activated by STIM could be due to constitutive closure of the pore and/or disruption of the interaction with STIM.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the functional defect.

claim: In the crystal of H206A Oraicryst, the cytosolic sides of two channels face one another and the M4-ext helices of different channels interact through anti-parallel coiled-coils.
source: In the crystal of H206A Oraicryst, the cytosolic sides of two channels face one another and the M4-ext helices of different channels interact through anti-parallel coiled-coils (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is an observation from the crystal packing shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The coiled-coil interactions in the H206A Oraicryst crystal are analogous to the pairing of M4-ext helices between adjacent subunits in the quiescent conformation.
source: These coiled-coil interactions are analogous to the pairing of M4-ext helices between adjacent subunits in the quiescent conformation (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Structures of WT Oraicryst and K163W Oraicryst were determined in the same crystal form (I41) as H206A Oraicryst.
source: To exclude the possibility that the crystal contacts in the H206A Oraicryst structure were responsible for the conformational changes we observed in the pore, we determined the structures of wild-type (WT) Oraicryst and K163W Oraicryst grown in the same crystal form (I41).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and is supported by crystallographic data.

claim: The structures of WT and K163W Oraicryst reveal an 'unlatched-closed' conformation of the channel.
source: The structures of WT and K163W Oraicryst reveal an 'unlatched-closed' conformation of the channel that resembles a hybrid of the quiescent and open conformations: the ion pores are closed as in the quiescent conformation but the M4/M4-ext regions have conformations like those observed in the H206A Oraicryst structure (Figure 9).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The unlatched-closed conformation has analogous straightenings of M4/M4-ext as the open structure.
source: The unlatched-closed conformation has analogous straightenings of M4/M4-ext as the open structure, and analogous crystal packing (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 8.

claim: The conformation of the M1-M4a portion of the channel in the unlatched-closed state is like the quiescent conformation.
source: The conformation of the M1-M4a portion of the channel, however, is like the quiescent conformation (Figure 9D), and as such, the pores of WT and K163W Oraicryst are closed and indistinguishable from the pore in the structure of the quiescent conformation (Figure 9B,D) (Hou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 9.

claim: Contacts within the crystal and the straightening of M4/M4-ext are not responsible for the opening of the pore observed with H206A Oraicryst.
source: Therefore, contacts within the crystal and the straightening of M4/M4-ext are not responsible for the opening of the pore that is observed with H206A Oraicryst.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that WT and K163W have similar crystal packing but closed pores.

claim: Anomalous difference electron density for an iron complex is observed in the basic region of the pore in the unlatched-closed conformation.
source: As in the quiescent conformation, anomalous difference electron density for an iron complex is observed in the basic region of the pore in the unlatched-closed conformation (Figure 9B, Figure 9—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by anomalous difference electron density data shown in Figure 9B and Figure 9—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The K163W mutation has no apparent effect on the structure other than removing the top ring of basic residues from the pore.
source: The K163W mutation has no other apparent effect, and this is analogous to observations from structures of the quiescent conformation with and without the K163W mutation (Hou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with the quiescent conformation.

claim: The presence of anomalous density in the basic region for both the quiescent and unlatched-closed conformations indicates that the pores share the same closed conformation.
source: The presence of the anomalous density in the basic region for both the quiescent and unlatched-closed conformations is further indication that the pores share the same closed conformation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of the iron complex in both conformations.

claim: An equilibrium exists between bent and unbent conformations of M4/M4-ext.
source: The X-ray structures of Orai suggest that an equilibrium exists between bent and unbent conformations of M4/M4-ext.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation of different M4/M4-ext conformations in different structures.

claim: STIM binding biases the equilibrium between bent and unbent conformations of M4/M4-ext in a cellular context.
source: Molecular constraints may bias this equilibrium during crystallization, and we hypothesize that STIM binding does so in a cellular context (as discussed later).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the role of STIM in channel activation.

claim: The M4b and M4-ext regions must undergo conformational changes for the pore to open.
source: Comparison of the structures of the quiescent, unlatched-closed and open conformations indicates that the M4b and M4-ext regions must undergo conformational changes for the pore to open.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural comparisons.

claim: In the quiescent conformation, M4b interacts with M3 as a result of the bend at Pro288.
source: As a result of the bend at Pro288 observed in the quiescent conformation, M4b interacts with M3 (Figure 1A, Figure 10A).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 10A.

claim: In the open structure, the interaction between M4b and M3 is no longer present due to the repositioning of M4b enabled by unbending at Pro288 and the unpairing of M4-ext helices.
source: In the open structure, the interaction between M4b and M3 is no longer present due to the repositioning of M4b that is enabled by unbending at Pro288 and the unpairing of M4-ext helices (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 10C.

claim: If the M4b-M3 interaction of the quiescent conformation were present, or if the M4-ext helices were paired, the rigid body motion of M1-M4a that underlies pore opening could not occur due to steric interference.
source: If the interaction between M4b and M3 of the quiescent conformation were present, or if the M4-ext helices were paired, the rigid body motion of M1-M4a that underlies pore opening could not occur due to steric interference between M3 and M4b (Figure 10D).
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling shown in Figure 10D.

claim: The paired M4-ext helices and the concomitant interactions between M4b and M3 of the quiescent conformation constitute 'latches' that must be released for the pore to open.
source: We conclude that the paired M4-ext helices and the concomitant interactions between M4b and M3 of the quiescent conformation constitute 'latches' that must be released for the pore to open.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural analysis.

claim: When the latches are fastened, they stabilize the pore in a closed conformation.
source: Thus, when the latches are fastened, they stabilize the pore in a closed conformation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural role of the latches.

claim: Complete straightenings of the M4/M4-ext helices may not be necessary for the pore to open.
source: Complete straightenings of the M4/M4-ext helices (e.g. analogous to the conformations of the M4/M4-ext helices observed in the structures of H206A, WT, and K163W Oraicryst) may not be necessary for the pore to open because there could be enough space for pore dilation with slight bends at the Pro288 and SHK hinges.
evidence: This is speculation based on structural considerations.

claim: The Pro288 and SHK hinges provide flexibility to M4b and M4-ext when the latches are released.
source: Rather than forming rigid helices, we hypothesize that the Pro288 and SHK hinges provide flexibility to M4b and M4-ext when the latches are released.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural role of these hinges.

claim: Release of the latches does not necessarily open the pore.
source: The structures of the unlatched-closed conformation reveal that release of the latches does not necessarily open the pore: the pore is closed despite the M4b and M4-ext helices adopting the same conformation that they do in the H206A structure.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural observation of the unlatched-closed conformation.

claim: While necessary, unlatching is not sufficient to open the pore.
source: Thus, while necessary, unlatching is not sufficient to open the pore.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that unlatched structures can have closed pores.

claim: Mutations that cause release of the latches may appear as activating mutations in a cellular context.
source: In a cellular context, mutations that cause release of the latches, that is, those that destabilize the quiescent conformation and/or favor unbending at the Pro288 or SHK hinges, may appear as activating mutations.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural role of the latches.

claim: Pro245 of human Orai1 (corresponding to Pro288 of Drosophila Orai) helps stabilize a closed state of the channel.
source: Congruently, Pro245 of human Orai1, which corresponds to Pro288 of Orai, has been characterized as a residue that helps stabilize a closed state of the channel - mutation to any other residue, which would favor straightening of the bend at this position, and thus destabilize a quiescent-like conformation, has an activating phenotype (Nesin et al., 2014; Palty et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: Certain mutations of human Orai1 within and around the SHK hinge create active channels.
source: Further, certain mutations of human Orai1 within and around the SHK hinge also create active channels (Zhou et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to functional studies.

claim: Mutations within the hydrophobic region of the pore give rise to leaky channels with diminished selectivity for Ca2+.
source: On the other hand, mutations within the hydrophobic region of the pore (e.g. F99C or V102A of human Orai1 or V174A of Orai) give rise to leaky channels, albeit with diminished selectivity for Ca2+ (Figure 7) (Hou et al., 2012; McNally et al., 2012; Yamashita et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by functional data and citations.

claim: The repositioning of the M1 helices in the opened pore indicates that the hydrophobic region widens markedly.
source: Although we cannot discern the conformations of amino acid side chains in the open structure, and thus there is a high degree of uncertainty when discussing the dimensions of the pore, the repositioning of the M1 helices in the opened pore indicates that the hydrophobic region widens markedly (Figure 11).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural changes shown in Figure 11.

claim: The hydrophobic region functions as a 'gate' that prevents or permits ion conduction.
source: We hypothesize that this widening, which accompanies the dramatic dilation of the basic region, is critical for ion permeation and that the hydrophobic region functions as a 'gate' – a variable constriction that prevents or permits ion conduction.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural observations.

claim: Direct coordination of Ca2+ by the ring of Glu178 residues in the selectivity filter is responsible for the channel's exquisite selectivity for Ca2+.
source: Ion binding in the open pore suggests that direct coordination of Ca2+ by the ring of Glu178 residues in the selectivity filter is responsible for the channel's exquisite selectivity for Ca2+.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the ion binding data.

claim: The proximity of the carboxylate moieties within the glutamate ring elevates the pKa values of the Glu178 side chains dramatically.
source: The proximity of the carboxylate moieties within the glutamate ring undoubtedly elevates the pKa values of the Glu178 side chains dramatically, such that they each would carry only a fraction of their −1 charge at physiological pH on average.
evidence: This is an inference based on electrostatic principles and supported by pKa calculations mentioned in the text.

claim: The selectivity filter of Orai toggles between having one and having two Ca2+ ions present in the physiological context.
source: In the physiological context of approximately 2 mM Ca2+ outside the cell, we suspect that the selectivity filter of Orai toggles between having one and having two Ca2+ ions present (although the two sites may have different free energies).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the ion selectivity mechanism.

claim: The M4-ext region of Orai interacts with a cytosolic portion of STIM that has a propensity to form coiled-coils.
source: Studies have shown that the M4-ext region of Orai interacts with a cytosolic portion of STIM that has a propensity to form coiled-coils (Kawasaki et al., 2009; Li et al., 2007; Muik et al., 2008; Park et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mutation of Ile316 and Leu319 in human Orai1 (L273S and L276D mutations) prevents the interaction of Orai1 with STIM1 and subsequent channel activation.
source: Mutation of the residues corresponding to Ile316 and Leu319 in human Orai1, which mediate the coiled-coil packing in the crystal structures, prevents the interaction of Orai1 with STIM1 and subsequent channel activation (L273S and L276D mutations of human Orai1) (Muik et al., 2008; Navarro-Borelly et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: Channel activation involves conformational changes in the M4-ext helices.
source: In accord with the unlatching we observe, an additional body of evidence suggests that channel activation involves conformational changes in the M4-ext helices (Navarro-Borelly et al., 2008; Palty et al., 2017; Tirado-Lee et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to other studies.

claim: Unlatching exposes the M4-ext regions and makes them available for interaction with STIM.
source: One possible mechanism of STIM binding is that unlatching would expose the M4-ext regions and make them available for interaction with STIM.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the mechanism of STIM binding.

claim: STIM1 can bind to loss-of-function mutants of human Orai1 that have constitutively closed pores.
source: Our observation that the unlatching of M4b from M3 does not necessarily open the pore is consistent with studies indicating that STIM1 can bind to loss-of-function mutants of human Orai1 that have constitutively closed pores, such as the pore-lining R91W mutant (Derler et al., 2009; McNally et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: The pore cannot open from the quiescent conformation directly.
source: An important finding from our work is that the pore cannot open from the quiescent conformation directly.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural analysis showing steric clashes.

claim: The activation of Orai by STIM must involve different conformations of M4/M4-ext than those observed in the quiescent structure.
source: Therefore, the activation of Orai by STIM must involve different conformations of M4/M4-ext than those observed in the quiescent structure.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural incompatibility of the quiescent conformation with pore opening.

claim: STIM activates the channel by binding to an unlatched conformation similar to what is observed in the unlatched-closed structure.
source: A logical hypothesis, which certainly requires further study, is that STIM activates the channel by binding to an unlatched conformation similar to what is observed in the unlatched-closed structure.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural findings.
